Jefferies said that despite management's optimism that its backlog continues to grow faster than revenue, Bloom Energy did not provide a formal backlog update.

JPMorgan also lowered its price target on Bloom, cutting it to $292 from $314 while maintaining an 'Overweight' rating.

The firm attributed the reduction to lower trading multiples among Bloom Energy's peer group, despite noting that its execution "continues to impress."

Bloom Energy Corp. (BE) shares suffered their steepest single-day decline in three months despite its third-quarter (Q3) results and fiscal year 2026 forecast surpassing Wall Street expectations.

According to TheFly, Jefferies lowered its price target on the fuel-cell power company, citing a lack of updates around delays tied to its largest opportunity with Oracle Corp. (ORCL).

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Bloom Energy shares closed over 11% lower on Friday, falling about 0.3% further during the afterhours session.

Source: Koyfin
Jefferies Flags Lack Of Updates On Oracle Opportunity

Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith lowered the firm's price target on Bloom Energy to $242 from $289 while maintaining a 'Hold' rating on the shares.

The target cut came after Bloom Energy raised its 2026 financial guidance for the third time this year.

Despite the company's management remaining optimistic that its backlog continues to grow faster than revenue, Bloom Energy did not provide a formal backlog update, Dumoulin-Smith said in a note.

Bloom Energy did highlight recent customer wins, but the analyst said those wins were already well known.

JPMorgan also lowered its price target on Bloom, cutting it to $292 from $314 while maintaining an 'Overweight' rating. The firm attributed the reduction to lower trading multiples among Bloom Energy's peer group, despite noting that its execution "continues to impress."

BTIG lowered its price target to $250 from $295 while maintaining a 'Buy' rating following the results. The firm pointed to a near-term margin drag as Bloom Energy ramps new production capacity and accommodates expedited customer timelines.

BTIG added that the cost of expanding manufacturing capacity is weighing on Bloom Energy's margin outlook.

Bloom Energy Reports Record Q3 Revenue

Bloom Energy reported record third-quarter revenue of $1.24 billion on Thursday, up 138.1% year over year, with product revenue rising 179.4% to $1.07 billion.

Gross margin increased to 33.8% from 29.2% a year earlier, while operating income rose to $225.4 million from $7.8 million. Its adjusted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $0.94, compared with 15 cents a year earlier.

title: This hot AI-fueled stock has been in a rut. It just beat earnings expectations by 36%.
detail:
This hot AI-fueled stock has been in a rut. It just beat earnings expectations by 36%.
Steve Goldstein
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 5:13 PM EDT 2 min read
ORCL
BE
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Bloom Energy's fuel cells have powered data centers. - Bloom Energy handout photo

A company that beat earnings expectations by 36% and revenue expectations by 15% would usually see a postresults bump. But not for Bloom Energy, the fuel-cell maker that has flourished due to data-center demand.

Bloom Energy BE late Thursday reported third-quarter earnings per share of 94 cents, up from just 15 cents a year earlier and comfortably ahead of the 69 cents that analysts polled by FactSet expected. Revenue rose 138% to $1.24 billion, beating expectations of $1.07 billion.

Bloom Energy said it is targeting between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion in revenue this year, versus the $4.26 billion consensus, while maintaining its adjusted gross margin outlook of 34%.

Its revenue guidance has been steadily increased by 41% since February, according to JPMorgan analysts.

The company, whose clients include Google GOOGL, Oracle ORCL and Nebius NBIS, burned $27 million in cash this quarter. "This quarter, we used cash from operations. But that is not the beginning of a trend," Bloom CFO Simon Edwards said, noting the company is cash-flow positive on the year. "We're balancing this margin expansion with also capturing the market opportunity in front of us," he added.

Chairman and CEO K.R. Sridhar referenced a comment from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who said that every quarter delay in a gigawatt data center translates to $10 billion of missed revenue. "So every 100-megawatt data center, a quarter delay would be a $1 billion lost revenue," said Sridhar. "That overwhelms every other value proposition that you will have on the power block."

Bloom Energy has also been highlighting fuel-cell use outside of artificial intelligence.

But the stock has been in a funk, down 38% from highs, through Thursday. It tumbled 11% on Friday, closing at a nearly three-month low.

"Good quarter, crowded trade, tough reaction" was the title of an analyst note from Citi's Vikram Bagri.

title: Can Manhattan Associates Stock Compound Your Money?

Can Manhattan Associates Stock Compound Your Money?

Manhattan Associates (MANH) stock has returned 59.7% since July 24, 2026, compared with 3.7% for the S&P 500. In the year before that run, the company kept buying back its own shares. It finished its latest four quarters with 59.0 million diluted shares, down from 62.4 million three years earlier. This reduction leaves each remaining share with a larger stake in the business. So how much has the shrinking share count added to what each of your shares earns?

Manhattan Associates' Earnings Per Share Outgrew Net Income

A shrinking share count has helped earnings per share grow faster than net income. Over the three years to June 2026, earnings per share climbed 14.6% a year, while net income increased 12.9% a year. Although the number of shares an investor holds remains the same, each one claims a larger portion of the profit.

In the past year, the buyback softened a decline instead. Net income fell 4.9% during the four quarters to June 2026, but earnings per share dropped a smaller 2.5%. Over those four quarters, the company spent $321 million more on buybacks than it issued in stock pay. That difference equals 2.3% of its market value at the October 22 close.

What Pays For Manhattan Associates' Buyback?

Most of this activity is funded by spare cash from a profitable software business. Over its latest four quarters, Manhattan Associates recorded an operating margin of 25.1%, compared with 18.5% for the S&P 500. Cash from operations reached $415 million, twice its net income. Capital spending consumed just 3.8% of that cash, leaving almost all of it as free cash flow.

The business generating that cash is still growing. Cloud revenue rose 26% to $127 million in fiscal Q2 2026. On the July 28, 2026 call, management said revenue already under contract but not yet booked reached $2.47 billion, up 23% from a year earlier.

Can Manhattan Associates Keep Buying Back At This Pace?

Not from free cash flow alone. Over the past four quarters, free cash flow covered 0.92 times the $435 million spent on buybacks, and the company paid no dividend. The rest came from its cash, which dropped to $186 million at the end of June 2026 from $231 million a year earlier. Even so, cash still exceeds debt by $132 million.

Each repurchased share also comes at a high price: the stock trades at 67.7 times earnings, compared with 23.0 for the S&P 500. As a result, every dollar spent retires a smaller slice of the company than it would at a lower price. The $225 million left under its share repurchase authority at the July 28 call would buy about 930,000 shares at the October 22 close of $242.17. In July, management also lowered its full-year GAAP operating margin forecast to 24.3% at the midpoint, down from 24.8%. This means a smaller share of each sales dollar is expected to remain as profit to pay for those purchases.

title: Bloom Energy Stock Sinks Despite Record Revenue and a Stellar Outlook. Is It Time to Buy?
detail:
Bloom Energy Stock Sinks Despite Record Revenue and a Stellar Outlook. Is It Time to Buy?
Neha Chamaria, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 2:03 PM EDT 4 min read
BE
ORCL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) delivered another blowout quarter, smashing estimates and growing profits faster than sales. Yet, its stock plunged after earnings and was down more than 12% as of Friday noon.

The company sells solid-oxide fuel cell servers that turn natural gas into electricity right at a customer's site. Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers desperately need that because the existing grid needs years to build additional capacity.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Bloom Energy can bypass the grid and swiftly deliver clean, reliable, 24/7 power to hyperscalers and data center operators. It delivered a complete fuel-cell system to Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) in 55 days last year. The tech giant was so impressed that it expanded its partnership for up to 2.8 gigawatts (GW) earlier this year.

So, what is happening with Bloom Energy stock? Why is it dropping like a rock – down 30% in one month, as of this writing?

Image source: Getty Images.

A bumper quarter and 2027 outlook

Revenue soared 138% year over year to a record $1.2 billion in the third quarter. Product sales, the fuel cell systems Bloom Energy ships to customers, topped $1 billion in sales in a single quarter for the first time.

Profit grew even faster. Adjusted operating margin jumped to 23.1% from 8.9% as revenue more than doubled while operating expenses rose only 26%. CFO Simon Edwards added that operating income in this single quarter surpassed what Bloom earned in all of 2025.

Then management raised its full-year revenue outlook for the third time this year. It now expects 2026 revenue of $4.5 billion, or about 122% growth.

Here's the kicker: Earlier in the year, Bloom Energy was guiding for a "humble" 60% revenue growth for the year. It has more than doubled its trajectory in just a couple of quarters.

So what's hurting the stock? The only metric I could find that may have miffed investors is cash burn. Bloom Energy posted negative free cash flow of $181 million in Q3.

Should investors worry? Hardly, because context is everything.

Is Bloom Energy stock a buy?

Demand is exploding, so Bloom Energy spent $153 million last quarter to scale up capacity as fast as possible. Data centers are built in phases, and Bloom is ready with its servers at each phase so operators don't have to wait.

That speed is everything for data centers.

1 software stock worth your attention and 2 we brush off

From commerce to culture, software is digitizing every aspect of our lives. This secular theme has materialized in superior earnings growth and stock price performance for most SaaS companies, and over the last six months, the industry's 54.6% return has topped the S&P 500 by 45.5 percentage points.

Nevertheless, investors should tread carefully as AI will commoditize many software products, and backing the wrong horse could result in hefty losses. Keeping that in mind, here is one software stock poised to generate sustainable market-beating returns and two we would avoid.

Two software stocks to sell:
UiPath (PATH)

Market Cap: $7.26 billion

Starting with robotic process automation (RPA) and evolving into a comprehensive automation powerhouse, UiPath (NYSE:PATH) provides an AI-powered business automation platform that enables organizations to create software robots that mimic human actions to streamline repetitive tasks and processes.

Why Does PATH Worry Us?

ARR growth averaged a weak 11.7% over the last year, suggesting that competition is pulling some attention away from its software

Estimated sales growth of 8.2% for the next 12 months implies demand will slow from its two-year trend

Extended payback periods on sales investments suggest the company's platform isn't resonating enough to drive efficient sales conversions

Oracle (ORCL)

Market Cap: $380.6 billion

Starting as a database company in 1977 and now powering mission-critical systems across the globe, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) provides enterprise software and hardware products and services that help businesses manage their information technology needs.

Why Does ORCL Give Us Pause?

Annual sales growth of 11.9% over the last five years lagged behind its software peers as its large revenue base made it difficult to generate incremental demand

Cash-burning history makes us doubt the long-term viability of its business model

Short cash runway increases the probability of a capital raise that dilutes existing shareholders

One software stock to watch:
HubSpot (HUBS)

Market Cap: $13.32 billion

Born from the idea that traditional interruptive marketing was becoming less effective, HubSpot (NYSE:HUBS) provides an integrated platform that helps businesses attract, engage, and manage customer relationships through marketing, sales, service, and content management tools.
